headline: New law lets schools in the federal school lunch program serve whole and 2% milk, and adds yearly food allergy training for cafeteria staff.
what_it_does: Schools in the National School Lunch Program may now offer whole, 2%, 1%, and fat-free milk, flavored or unflavored, organic or not. Before this, federal rules allowed only 1% and fat-free milk. Fat in milk no longer counts toward the school meal limit on saturated fat, and schools may offer nondairy drinks that are nutritionally similar to milk. School food service workers must also receive training on food allergies and get certified every year.

who_it_affects.how: They may be offered whole or 2% milk and nondairy drinks that are nutritionally similar to milk, in addition to low-fat and fat-free milk.

who_it_affects.group: Parents and legal guardians of students with disabilities that limit their diet
who_it_affects.how: They can now give the school a written statement to get a milk substitute for their child, instead of needing one from a licensed doctor.

who_it_affects.group: Schools and school food service programs
who_it_affects.how: They get more milk choices, no longer have to match milk to the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, and do not count milk fat when checking that meals meet the saturated fat limit.

who_it_affects.group: School cafeteria and food service workers
who_it_affects.how: They must take training on preventing, spotting, and responding to food allergic reactions and get certified in their training every year.
Schools may now buy whole and 2% milk, which were not allowed before under federal school lunch rules.

when_it_takes_effect: Signed into law January 14, 2026; the summary does not give a separate start date.
